newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Southern Albania edges towards midnight deadline.
newsitem.headline: Southern Albania edges towards midnight deadline.

text.p: Rebel-held towns in southern Albania edged on Thursday towards their midnight deadline for the resignation of President Sali Berisha, without any obvious plan of action if he refuses.
Rebel representatives met opposition political leaders in the southern stronghold of Gjirokaster but had little to add to their demand that Berisha resign, "or else."
A rebel commander from the mining town of Memalija, Gjolek Malaj, told reporters in Gjirokaster that fifty men were on their way to Tirana to put the President under house arrest.
"Speaking as an individual, if Berisha does not resign we are prepared to send people to bombard him," Malaj added.
His boast provoked incredulity and unease from some other leaders gathered in Gjirokaster.
"We do not support any military move to overthrow Berisha. We think he can and should be removed by legal, peaceful means," said Paskal Milo, Vice-Chairman of Albania's small Social Democratic Party.
"In the end, events will make Berisha step down. It will not be a personal decision because if it were up to him personally he would be president for life."
Rebel leaders from 13 southern Albanian towns and some opposition political leaders are scheduled to meet in Tepelene on Friday to plot their next move.
If, as expected, Berisha is still in power, a Presidential Council is likely to be formed as a shadow government.

The south is united only in its lawlessness and opposition to Berisha, who is blamed for the recent collapse of pyramid schemes which bankrupted many Albanian families. The north of the country remains under government control.
Although citizens' councils have been formed to co-ordinate day-to-day affairs in southern towns, actual power rests with local mafias now army and police units have been dissolved.
Both the government and the south lack the strength to impose their will on one another. Stalemate or political compromise seem the only options.

Observers scented a possible political deal in the offing on Wednesday when Bashkim Fino, prime minister in the new coalition government formed in the wake of the pyramid scandal, was scheduled to go south to meet rebel leaders.

As Mayor of the southern town of Gjirokaster and a member of the opposition Socialist Party, Fino seemed the man to broker a rapprochement with the rebels and clear the way for fresh national elections in June.
But the Prime Minister's visit was cancelled, perhaps for security reasons.
It may have been just as well since many Albanians in the south doubt Fino's motives and seem terminally suspicious of any government initiative from Tirana.
The comments of 25-year old Ardian, an unemployed man in the southern port city of Sarande, are typical:

"The similarities between Fino and Berisha are greater than the differences. They were schemers together smuggling oil from Albania into Montenegro and Serbia during the Bosnian war. What we have now is the same government with different faces."
Another unemployed man, Vangjel Xhani, added: "Berisha is like a knight in armour on a horse. So long as he stays on the horse of government he is strong. The moment he is knocked off he is dead."
